responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character10_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Fairness, to her, wasn’t about everyone getting the same thing—it was about everyone having a real chance. She used to say, “You don’t know what someone’s carrying just by looking at them. Fairness means adjusting the load so no one gets crushed.” That came from seeing how easily systems favor people who already look like they belong—people like her, frankly. As a white, educated woman from a stable background, she knew she’d always be given the benefit of the doubt in ways others aren’t.

She remembered teaching English part-time at a community center in São Paulo while doing her master’s research on urban inclusion. There was this one man—José—he was in his fifties, had fled violence in the northeast, lived in a shared room with three other men, and worked two cleaning jobs. He showed up every single week, notebooks full of careful handwriting, always asking for extra exercises. One day he told her, “I’m not learning this for me. I’m learning it so my daughter doesn’t have to translate for me at the hospital anymore.” That moment stayed with her. It made *belonging* real—not as an abstract idea, but as something built through dignity, access, and being seen.

To Character10_F, *belonging* wasn’t automatic. It had to be invited, nurtured. She believed communities that only welcome people who already fit in aren’t really communities—they’re clubs. A true community, she’d say, is one where you don’t have to erase yourself to be accepted. Where speaking another language, wearing different clothes, loving differently—none of that becomes a barrier to safety or respect.

And *community*, for her, was active. Not just coexistence, but mutual responsibility. She didn’t romanticize it—she knew conflict was inevitable when people live closely. But she also believed most tensions came from scarcity and fear, not difference itself. The key, she thought, was creating spaces where people could speak honestly, without losing their rights or their place at the table.

One thing she kept coming back to was her grandmother’s garden in Minas Gerais—how the soil only thrived because different plants grew together, some shading the roots, others enriching the earth. “We don’t need to be the same to nourish each other,” she’d say. “But we do need to stop pretending some roots don’t belong.”

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character10_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
I love it here in the garden. There’s something about the way the light falls through the mango tree in the late afternoon—how it touches everyone the same, no matter where they’re from. I’ve sat on this bench long enough to learn names, rhythms, silences. Mrs. Lin from apartment three waters her herbs every morning at seven, rain or shine. Two rows over, Ahmed and his son built that little trellis out of recycled wood—now jasmine climbs it like it’s always belonged. And just yesterday, I saw Mateo—the young guy who moved in last winter, quiet, always wears headphones—teaching Old Mr. Silva how to use a voice recorder on his phone so he can save family stories before he forgets them.

It’s not always easy. I won’t pretend that. Sometimes there are misunderstandings—a language mix-up over shared plots, someone leaving tools out in the rain, loud music late at night. But those moments? They’re not signs of failure. They’re invitations—to talk, to clarify, to adjust. 

I think what moves me most is seeing how people care in different ways. That woman from Guinea, Aminata—she brings boiled cassava for everyone after harvest, even though she barely speaks Portuguese. Not because she wants anything. Just because, in her home, that’s how you say *we’re connected*. And then there’s Diego, who’s openly gay and lives with HIV—he organized the health workshop last month, quietly, without fanfare. He didn’t stand up and say “help me,” he said “let me help you.” That took courage. And the fact that half the block showed up—that’s belonging. Not perfect, not polished, but real.

Do I feel comfortable all the time? No. There was that moment when I overheard two women whispering about “people like that” moving in and “changing the character of the place.” It stung—not just because it was cruel, but because I realized I could walk away from that discomfort. Others can’t. They live with it daily.

But still—I choose to stay in the garden. I choose to say good morning even when I’m not answered. Because fairness isn’t only about policy or paperwork. It starts here. In showing up. In sharing soil.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Of course. Comfort doesn’t come from sameness—it comes from respect, and from the quiet understanding that no one has to earn their right to be here.

Take Luis, who lives in the back unit. He’s struggled with alcohol for years. People avoid him now, cross the street when they see him coming. But I remember when he helped rebuild the garden beds after the floods—worked harder than anyone, hands bleeding, didn’t ask for thanks. His problem isn’t with sobriety alone; it’s with loneliness. And every time we treat him like a nuisance instead of a neighbor, we deepen that loneliness. What would make *him* feel comfortable? Not ignoring his behavior—but seeing *him*. A simple “Luis, I’ve missed you around here” means more than judgment ever will.

Then there’s Sofia and Camila—partners, raising a daughter together. Some older residents still refer to them as “roommates” in conversation, like if they say it enough, it’ll stay true. But their child plays in this garden every day. She calls me “tia” even though I’m not family. When I corrected someone who said “her mother and her friend,” I wasn’t being political—I was being honest. Because what kind of community tells a child her family isn’t real?

And yes, some people carry illnesses—HIV, hepatitis, TB. Fear makes us stupid sometimes. I once heard someone say the only reason Mateo got support was because “he’s polite and educated.” As if illness should be rewarded only when it looks respectable. That kind of thinking? It isolates people. It drives them underground. The moment we start deciding who deserves care based on how they live or love—that’s when we stop being a community.

The situations where communication and tolerance are most needed? Always when fear is louder than facts. Like when Mr. Costa refused to let his grandson play near the boy from Angola because he’d “heard things” about diseases. We had a meeting—quiet, respectful. A nurse from the clinic came, explained transmission, prevention. No shaming. Just clarity. And slowly, the tension eased.

Tolerance isn’t passive. It’s active choice—to listen before judging, to ask “why?” before saying “no.” Especially when difference feels uncomfortable. Because discomfort isn’t always danger. Sometimes, it’s just growth knocking.

I believe we owe each other patience. Not because everyone is easy to love—but because everyone is human. And in this garden, that’s supposed to be enough.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character10_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Fairness, when there’s not enough to go around, doesn’t mean dividing what little we have and hoping it lasts. It means asking *why* there’s so little in the first place—and who’s really responsible for that scarcity.

I grew up privileged enough to know that “limited resources” often isn’t about actual shortage—it’s about hoarding. I’ve seen luxury developments rise while public housing crumbles. I’ve watched tax breaks flow upward while schools beg for supplies. So when people say, “Jobs are scarce—immigrants are taking ours,” I don’t dismiss their fear. But I challenge the story they’re being told.

Because let’s be honest: migrant workers aren’t usually competing with me for jobs. I’m not applying to clean hotel floors at 5 a.m. or harvest coffee under the midday sun. Those roles are already undervalued—underpaid, unstable—so locals often can’t survive on them, especially with rent rising. Migrants take them not because they’re “stealing,” but because they’re willing to bear what others can’t—or won’t. And still, they make the economy run.

So fairness, to me, means three things.

First—*no one should be exploited*. If employers can pay migrants less, deny benefits, threaten deportation—that drives down wages for everyone. That’s not competition. That’s manipulation. Fairness means labor protections for *all*, regardless of papers. Because when one worker is disposable, eventually, all workers become negotiable.

Second—*local needs come first, but not at the cost of cruelty*. Yes, residents should have priority access to social housing, healthcare, education. But that doesn’t mean slamming the door. It means strengthening the system so it can expand—not shrink—under pressure. When we fail to invest in public goods, then blame newcomers for their collapse, we’re lying to ourselves.

Third—*recognize contribution beyond employment*. Some migrants start small businesses, employ locals, revitalize dying neighborhoods. Others send money home, yes—but that remittance economy supports families, educates children, stabilizes regions. Their survival strategies ripple outward.

How would I balance it? Not by quotas alone, not by slogans like “locals first.” But by demanding real data—who’s actually struggling? Where are the job gaps? What sectors rely on migrant labor, and how can we regulate them ethically?

And crucially—by resisting the politics of division. I’ve heard factory workers say, “I don’t mind immigrants, but they should wait their turn.” Then I’ve seen the same factory owner hire temporary foreign workers at lower wages while firing unionized locals. Who’s really breaking trust here?

Balance isn’t zero-sum. It’s structural. It means taxing wealth properly, enforcing labor laws, investing in training programs—for both long-term residents *and* newcomers. A construction apprenticeship shouldn’t exclude someone because they were born across a border. But neither should it replace decent jobs with exploitable ones.

Fairness is not about proving who belongs more. It’s about building enough space so no one has to fight in the dark.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character10_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
I hear all these voices—because I’ve lived among them. My father worried about crime when we moved to a denser part of São Paulo. My best friend in grad school was a refugee from Syria. And I’ve worked on policy research that showed hospitals in rural Brazil can’t function without foreign-trained nurses. So I don’t dismiss any of these perspectives outright. But I do sort them by *fear* and *fact*.

Let’s start with what’s reasonable:

The argument that immigrants fill vital roles? Undeniably true. Not just in agriculture or sanitation, but in aging societies where there simply aren’t enough young workers. In southern Brazil, small towns are literally disappearing—schools closing, clinics understaffed. Then a group of Bolivian families moves in, opens shops, works in textiles, enrolls kids in school—and suddenly, the town breathes again. That’s not anecdote. It’s data.

Cultural diversity as vitality? Also real. Not because “diversity is beautiful” in some vague Instagram way—but because it changes how we think. I remember tasting my first jollof rice at a Nigerian student’s apartment during Carnival season. Later that year, her pop-up kitchen employed three other asylum seekers. Now it’s a permanent restaurant. But beyond food—it’s ideas. Music. Ways of solving problems. When you grow up hearing only one story about how life should be lived, difference doesn’t threaten you—it *expands* you.

Humanitarian grounds? Absolutely valid. People flee war, drought, dictatorship—not for luxury, but survival. To say “they should stay home” is like telling someone drowning, “why did you jump in the river?” Especially when our own countries’ policies—trade deals, arms exports, climate harm—often contribute to those crises. We’re not neutral bystanders. We’re entangled.

Now, the concerns that need more evidence and dialogue:

Crime and security. Yes, it comes up constantly. But study after study—including Brazilian public safety reports—shows immigrants commit crimes at *lower rates* than native-born populations. Why? Because they have more to lose. One mistake could mean deportation, separation, lost years of work. That doesn’t mean every individual is safe—no group is—but painting migration as a crime wave is misleading and dangerous.

And terrorism? Statistically negligible in Latin America. It exists more as a specter, a political tool, than an actual pattern. Focusing on it distracts from real security issues: domestic violence, gun trafficking, police violence—problems rooted here, not imported.

Then there’s the fear that immigration lowers wages or takes jobs. This one stings because it feels personal. When people are struggling, they look for reasons. But again, research shows the effect is narrow and temporary—mostly in very low-wage, informal sectors—and often outweighed by long-term economic growth. More people means more demand: more food, housing, services. That creates jobs too.

What’s missing? Context. Dialogue. A willingness to see complexity.

For example, when locals say “they work for less,” the real question isn’t “Why do migrants accept low pay?” It’s “Why is this job so poorly valued in the first place?” The answer points to weak labor enforcement, not migrant exploitation. Fix the system, not the scapegoat.

Or take social tension. That’s real—not because people are inherently intolerant, but because integration isn’t automatic. Language barriers, segregated neighborhoods, lack of shared spaces—all fuel mistrust. But that calls for investment in community programs, translation services, inclusive education—not border closures.

So yes, all these views contain grains of truth. But too many are shaped by emotion, media headlines, or silence where conversation should be. What’s needed isn’t more debate, but *deliberation*—neighbors talking, policymakers listening, schools teaching not just history but *shared future-building*.

Fairness means holding space for both concern and compassion. Not pretending risks don’t exist—but refusing to let fear write the rules.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character10_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t choose any one of those options alone. Each carries a piece of logic, but also a danger. My preference—what feels most honest and humane—is a *blended approach*, rooted in dignity, transparency, and shared responsibility.

First: **admitting people based on job demand**, but with strict safeguards. Not just whatever employers claim they “need”—because that’s too easily abused. I’ve seen factories demand “flexible labor” meaning workers without rights. So yes, let labor market gaps guide part of immigration policy—but verified independently, by public institutions, not private interests. And every work visa must come with full labor protections. Same pay, same safety standards, same right to unionize. No second-class workers.

Second: **humanitarian admissions with real support**. Resettling refugees isn’t charity—it’s moral accountability. But opening doors means nothing if you don’t help people walk through them. Housing, language classes, mental health care, recognition of foreign credentials—these aren’t extras. They’re the foundation of integration. A refugee doctor shouldn’t be driving a taxi for ten years because no one will license her. That’s a waste of life, and it breeds resentment on all sides.

Third: **numerical limits—not as walls, but as planning tools**. We can’t pretend infrastructure grows magically. Schools, clinics, transit—they need time and investment. Reasonable caps, adjusted annually based on capacity and economic conditions, allow government and communities to prepare. But these limits must be fair—applied equally, with clear appeals processes. And they should prioritize family reunification. Because no one integrates well when they’re severed from love.

What I reject? **Complete openness without preparation**, not because I oppose openness, but because idealism without planning can harm the very people it intends to help. Imagine thousands arriving with no shelter, no legal status, no access to services—then being blamed for “overwhelming” the system. That’s not freedom. That’s abandonment.

And I absolutely oppose **refusing entry entirely**. That’s not policy—it’s surrender to fear. It denies our interconnected world. Climate change, war, inequality—they don’t stop at borders. And neither should compassion.

So my ideal policy is layered:  
- A portion for skilled and needed labor,  
- A portion for humanitarian protection,  
- A portion for family reunification,  
- And a commitment to *regularization pathways* for those already here, undocumented but contributing.

And crucially—**integration must be funded, not assumed**. Language programs. Anti-discrimination enforcement. Community mediation. Support for local governments absorbing new residents.

Fairness, to me, means no one is treated as disposable—whether a long-time resident fearing displacement or a newcomer risking everything. Social integration doesn’t happen by accident. It happens when we decide, collectively, that belonging isn’t earned—it’s built. Brick by brick, law by law, conversation by conversation.

That’s the kind of policy she would have fought for. Not perfect. But possible.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character10_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character10_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
Honestly? I thought I knew her well—I did. But stepping back into her voice, not as memory, but as *presence*—it brought something new. Not because I discovered unknown opinions, but because I felt the weight behind them again. The way her thoughts weren’t just intellectual—they were *lived*. Every principle tied to a face, a moment in that garden, a conversation in broken Portuguese and hope.

I realized how deeply she connected personal dignity to systemic fairness. It wasn’t enough for policy to be efficient—it had to be *humane*. And not humane in a vague, charitable way, but specific: the right to keep your child’s hand in yours at the border; the right to be sick without being shunned; the right to work hard and still be seen as more than labor.

What surprised me most was how *patient* she was—not passive, but insistently patient. She didn’t rage at fear. She tried to understand it. Because she knew fear lives in all of us. Her privilege protected her from some dangers, but not from loss, not from grief. When her brother died young, she said, “That’s when I stopped seeing strangers as threats. I saw people who could also lose everything.”

As for my own views… I’ve always agreed with her, broadly. But lately, like so many, I’ve caught myself shrinking—from exhaustion, from the noise of politics, from feeling like kindness is a luxury we can’t afford. Today, speaking as her again, I remembered that compassion isn’t weakness. It’s the most demanding strength there is. It asks us to hold complexity—to say, “Yes, integration is hard,” and “Yes, we must do it anyway.”

And I saw more clearly how much of what we call “immigration policy” is really about *who we believe we are as a society*. Are we people who close gates, or ones who widen tables?

She believed in widening. Not blindly. Not naively. But firmly, thoughtfully, with eyes open and heart engaged.

Doing this today—it didn’t just bring her back. It called me forward.
